concept.body: Composite solids price by decomposition: split at the seams (a silo = cylinder + hemisphere; a capsule's two hemispherical caps = one sphere), apply the justified formula to each piece, and ADD. Matched radii make seams clean — no gaps or overlaps to correct.

widget.prompt: Cylinder (radius 2, height 6) plus hemisphere (radius 2). Total coefficient of π (2 decimals) = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 24 is the cylinder alone — the dome adds ⅔(2³) = 16/3 ≈ 5.33: total ≈ 29.33.
34.67 caps with a FULL sphere (32/3) — half is 16/3: ≈ 29.33.

steps.body: Real objects are compounds: a silo is a cylinder wearing a hemisphere; a capsule is a cylinder with hemispherical caps. Volume ADDS across a clean joint — decompose, price each piece with the justified formulas, sum. The only skill is seeing the seam.

widget.prompt: Why should the hemisphere and cylinder of a silo share the same radius at the join?

options.label: To make one continuous circular seam.
options.feedback: Right. Equal radii make the outer surfaces meet at one continuous circular seam. The volumes would still add if the radii differed.

options.label: Because hemispheres have only one radius.
options.feedback: Hemispheres come in any radius. The radius match controls whether the joined outside surface is continuous.

options.label: To make the component volumes additive.
options.feedback: Non-overlapping component volumes add whether or not the radii match. Different radii leave a ledge at the join.

options.label: To make the component volumes equal.
options.feedback: The components can have different volumes. Equal radii are needed for a continuous circular join, not equal volume.

steps.body: Find the join by measuring it.

widget.prompt: Sweep a section through the sphere, with a constant-area prism beside it for reference. Test several heights, then stop where the sphere's section matches the prism's — that height is where a hemisphere can be joined cleanly.
widget.successFeedback: Only at the equator does the sphere's section reach πr² — everywhere else it is smaller. That is exactly why the cylinder's radius must equal the hemisphere's: the join is a shared circle, and the hemisphere's widest circle is the only one that can match a cylinder's constant section. Mismatch the radii and the two solids meet along a step, not a surface, and the volumes stop simply adding.
widget.positionFeedback: Keep sweeping, then settle at the height where the two section areas agree. On a sphere that happens at one height only.
widget.comparisonFeedback: Bring in the constant-area prism. “Same radius at the join” is a COMPARISON, so both sections have to be on screen to be compared.
widget.invariantFeedback: Move the plane through several heights first. The point is that the sphere's section keeps changing while the prism's does not — one snapshot cannot show that.

predict.prompt: A hemisphere of radius 5 sits on a cylinder. Across how many heights does the sphere's horizontal section have area π·5²?

options.label: One — the equator, and nowhere else
Every height — the radius is 5 throughout
None — a curved surface never gives a flat circle

predict.reveal: A sphere's sections are circles that shrink as you move away from the equator, so π·5² is reached exactly once. The equator is therefore the only circle a cylinder of radius 5 can be joined to — which is why the two radii must match.

widget.prompt: A composite of a cylinder (radius 5, height h) plus a matching hemisphere has total volume 775π/3. The hemisphere holds 250π/3 (chapter 3's number). The cylinder's height h = ?

commonErrors.feedback: 10.33 ≈ (775/3)/25 skips removing the dome — the cylinder holds 775/3 − 250/3 = 175, so h = 175/25 = 7.

takeaways: Composite volume = sum of the pieces across clean (matched-radius) seams.
Standard compounds: silo (cylinder + hemisphere), capsule (cylinder + sphere-in-two-halves), ice-cream (cone + hemisphere).
Reverse problems: subtract known pieces to expose the unknown dimension.
